Q16823902.summary: In the arched central panel Christ hangs on the cross, head bowed and wearing a loincloth, between the Virgin and Saint John, while half-length archangels lean in above the arms of the cross. On the folding wings, standing saints, many of them soldier saints, are carved in pairs in two tiers. Polished and elegant, the triptych is a fine example of the ivories made in 10th-century Constantinople for private devotion.
facts: The Greek inscription above the Virgin and John reads 'Behold thy son; behold thy mother', Christ's words from the cross.
It belongs to the 'Romanos group' of ivories closely connected with the Byzantine imperial court, alongside the Harbaville Triptych in the Louvre.
It was bequeathed to the British Museum by Charles Borradaile in 1923 (registration 1923,1205.1); the suggestion that it was made for Anna Porphyrogenita cannot be substantiated.
Q16823902.notes: Wikidata gives 9th century; Wikipedia and the British Museum record cited on Commons give 900–1000. Corrected to 10th century.

cur:manuscripts-san-paolo-bible-apocalyp.summary: Within a city of towers and arcades, angels watch from above and below as the Lamb steps toward an altar draped in purple, on which rests the sealed book; beside it, the evangelist symbols lift a veil from a seated elder. As in the earlier Tours Bibles, Christ appears as the Lamb who opens the book of the Revelation.
facts: Of all surviving Carolingian Bibles, this is the most thoroughly illuminated, with 24 surviving full-page miniatures, including a Christ in Majesty and this Apocalypse frontispiece.

It was presented to Pope John VIII at Charles the Bald's imperial coronation on Christmas 875 and was given to the abbey of Saint Paul outside the Walls under Gregory VII; its text was written by a monk named Ingobert.
